A snob is a person who believes — consciously or not — that they are better than others, and who makes this belief visible through the way they treat people. They constantly rank human beings on an invisible scale of "superior" and "inferior," and they behave accordingly: looking down on those they consider beneath them, and eagerly flattering or admiring those they consider above them.

The word is always used as a criticism. Nobody proudly calls themselves a snob. When you call someone a snob, you are pointing out a flaw in their character.
The Two Directions a Snob Operates In

To truly understand a snob, you need to see that they operate in two directions simultaneously:

1. Downward — Contempt for the "inferior"
A snob treats people they consider lower (in wealth, status, education, taste, etc.) with coldness, dismissiveness, or barely hidden disrespect. They might ignore them, speak to them in a condescending tone, or simply act as if those people don't quite matter.

2. Upward — Admiration for the "superior"
At the same time, a snob eagerly seeks the approval of people they consider higher or more prestigious. They want to associate with the "right" people, attend the "right" events, and be seen in the "right" places.

This two-directional behaviour — looking down and looking up — is the hallmark of a snob.
What a Snob Bases Their Superiority On

Here is what makes the word flexible and widely applicable: a snob can base their sense of superiority on almost anything. It doesn't have to be wealth or social class. Whatever a person values deeply, they can become a snob about it.

  • Social/Class snob — Looks down on people with less money, a lower-status job, or a less prestigious background. They might subtly mock someone for taking public transport, or treat a waiter as an inconvenience rather than a person.
  • Intellectual snob — Looks down on people they consider less educated or less intelligent. They make others feel stupid for not knowing something, or they roll their eyes at "simple" or "popular" ideas.
  • Food snob — Dismisses people who eat "common" food. They act horrified if you enjoy fast food or instant noodles, and they cannot have a conversation about food without subtly implying that most people's tastes are unsophisticated.
  • Music snob — Looks down on people who listen to popular or mainstream music. They believe their taste (usually in obscure or classical music) is far superior, and they let people know it.
  • Literary snob — Dismisses readers of genre fiction, bestsellers, or "lowbrow" books. They only respect certain authors and make others feel embarrassed for what they read.
  • Wine snob / Coffee snob — Makes people feel inferior about what they drink. They turn a simple choice of beverage into a test of sophistication that most people are quietly expected to fail.

In every case, the structure is the same: I have refined taste / high status / superior knowledge, and you do not, and that makes me better than you.
How a Snob Behaves in Practice

Snobbery doesn't always look dramatic. It is often quiet and subtle. Here are some common behaviours:

  • Name-dropping: Casually mentioning prestigious people, brands, schools, or places they are connected to — not to share information, but to establish their status. ("Oh, I was just at the Tate Modern with the director last week...")
  • Condescending tone: Speaking to "lesser" people in a tone that is slightly too patient, as if they are explaining things to a child.
  • Visible disapproval: A small sigh, a raised eyebrow, or a brief pause when they hear your choice of music, restaurant, or holiday destination.
  • Excluding people: Deliberately making someone feel like an outsider — that they don't belong in a particular group, conversation, or space.
  • Praising the "right" things excessively: Going on at length about the superiority of certain brands, schools, art forms, or experiences — with the unspoken message being that people who cannot access these things are lacking.

• "Don't mind her — she's a terrible snob who refuses to eat at any restaurant that hasn't been reviewed in a magazine."
  • "He's an intellectual snob who makes you feel foolish for watching television."
  • "The new manager turned out to be a class snob; he was charming to the senior staff but barely acknowledged the junior employees."

• Snobbish / Snobby (adjective): Describing the behaviour or attitude. "She gave me a snobbish look when I mentioned where I went to school."
  • Snobbery (noun): The behaviour or quality of being a snob. "The snobbery in that club is insufferable."
  • Snobbishness (noun): Same as snobbery, slightly more formal. "His snobbishness drove most people away."
The Most Important Thing to Remember

The deepest truth about a snob is not just that they look down on people — it's that their sense of self-worth depends on feeling superior. A snob is not confident in themselves independently; they need a hierarchy, and they need to feel they are near the top of it. Remove the hierarchy, and the snob becomes insecure.

This is why snobbery is considered not just unpleasant but also somewhat pitiable by those who understand it well. The snob's contempt for others reveals, more than anything else, an anxiety about their own worth.
